title: I made a free browser game where you ARE the dungeon—looking for feedback on the first 5 minutes
author: LikeMyGame
selftext:
The adventurers are here for treasure. You’d really prefer they leave.

I’m making **We Are Dungeon!**, a single-player game where you’re a living dungeon defending your Heart. You match magical runes to create monsters, traps, and other defenses, then deploy them along the adventurers’ route.

**Play free in your browser:**  
[We Are Dungeon! on itch.io](https://likemygame.itch.io/we-are-dungeon)

Please try it on a PC, use fullscreen, and start with **The First Awakening**, the guided tutorial.

I enjoy playing it, but I’ve spent so much time building and testing it that I can’t reliably judge what makes sense to a new player. If you have five minutes, I’d love to hear:

**Where did you first become unsure what to do—or lose the desire to continue?**

If something made you want to keep playing, I’d like to hear that too. You don’t need to finish a run or write a detailed review. Even “I stopped here because…” would help.

For the AI development side: the design and iteration are mine, and I use AI for code and artwork. The current 3D assets are from KayKit. I know they are lacking severely and I have my eye on some other options, but want to ensure this game is something people actually want to play before dropping hundreds of more dollars into it as this is a passion project with a budget. 😅 

One thing I've noticed throughout this process, though less so as the models evolve, is that bunching requests together, even though they seem related in my mind, can cause confusion to the AI agent. Hence, the many, MANY iterations. Like when I added low ground fog to the 3D view, it sometimes formed hallways that didn’t exist: fog drifted across empty void and connected rooms that weren’t linked. I compared screenshots of the 2D map and the 3D overhead view side by side. That made it clear the fog was laid out as a top-to-bottom mirror image of the real dungeon, caused by an image-flip default in the graphics code, and the fix was a single setting. The lesson: my test dungeon was nearly symmetrical, so it hid the bug, and I now test visual features on a large, lopsided dungeon before calling them done.

I’m looking for honest feedback to help decide what to improve next. I’ll check back at least once a day and reply. Thanks for giving it a try!

comments.author: Smalltime-studios
comments.body: This looks great!  I'm heading over to go play it now!  Awesome stuff!

replies.author: Smalltime-studios
replies.body:
OK Great initial UI/UX.  I could understand pretty well the setup and the minigame (Bejeweled like) for unlocking "things" the adventurers would encounter. 

I awoken the dungeon and saw things moving.  I switched to 3D view and saw the models, but they just walked, and then frolicked in each room.  I didnt know if my setup did damage to them, they did damage to the traps, or otherwise... they just kind of frolicked in each room and then moved to the next. 

Some kind of player feedback here would be great.  Spawning a skeleton and showing it dying if they defeat the skeleton, or a trap door springing up, or something to indicate what is happening to the adventurers for the player to easily understand... and how effective (or not effective) it is.

Great start though!  I really see where this could go and it's fun to play the "other side" be being a dungeon trying to stop attackers!

replies.body: Interesting. Did you play the tutorial? Are you saying you placed a rite (trap or other item) into a room and it didn't activate when the adventurers arrived? There should be notices about damage in the log and you should it reflected in the adventurer profile.

comments.author: AsparagusOk8818
comments.body:
Utterly impenetrable. 

  
Please, people. Having a dense and complex interface is not the same thing as having a deep and rich game, and having your alleged tutorial immediately bombard the screen with ten million buttons and visual elements defeats its purpose.

replies.author: LikeMyGame
replies.body:
In fairness, there are many popular game, X4 easily comes to mind, that have a FAR...galaxy spanning more complex interface. Granted, that game is much larger in scope.

What is so "complex" about the interface? The main pieces are the 1) map to track where the adventures are inside you and 2) the ritual forge to create new playable rites/actions and 3) the rite rack that stores the playable action. 

The tutorial "bombards you" with the actual game and then takes you step by step highlighting what to do and why, which is the purpose of a tutorial.

Thanks for...taking the time to give feedback so weak that not even a divine being could use it for any purpose...?

replies.author: AsparagusOk8818
replies.body:
https://preview.redd.it/3hc53h0ldbwh1.png?width=1917&format=png&auto=webp&s=a90fef13d7a9a3bc41169532ef4c44495eb12c36

  
Just look at this screenshot. This is step one of the tutorial, dude. There's no directionality, and the screen is completely packed with esoteric information. Big row of buttons on the right, big grid in the center, space on the right that, the moment you click continue, fills with esoteric symbol blocks, row of portraits on top, purple bar to the left of that... 

Are you seriously going to compare this browser game to X4? Is this your north star for this browser game? Are you making a Dungeon Keeper equivalent to X4? 

And no, going into the tutorial for X4, if memory serves, did not instantly provide me with a screen full of buttons and UI elements with zero context for what any of it is or does.  
  
Mask out the unnecessary elements. Introduce concepts one thing at a time. Don't just accept that Claude built an interface, shrug, and tell the machine to use the whole fckn interface for the tutorial. That's not how tutorials work. 

  
So, sure, if you want actionable critique: Claude over-built the UI; you should not have accepted it just because it looked nice. It needs to expose fewer visual elements at once to be usable and approachable, and the tutorial needs to expose the minimal possible information at a time to the player so that they can slowly acclimate to the game's systems. 

Claude can build you a great-looking UI, but it won't (yet) know the difference between good aesthetics and good functionality.

replies.author: LikeMyGame
replies.body:
Now that is some actionable, and much appreciated feedback! Huzzah! I will say that X4 isn't my north star, but it is an example of a game with a much higher learning curve, but is still commercially viable...not for the faint of heart! I suppose, in a way, I wanted to make a game that had a depth of mechanics. Some real meat on its bones. You have to be into that kind of game which won't be for everyone.

Now, I can see how having the full UI visible during the tutorial could be overwhelming...possibly. I'm honestly torn on whether or not to address this as the fact they can't follow the prompt on the forefront which has explicit instructions and a "Continue" button means this game might not be for them. Which is fair and fine.

This UI is much more improved and streamlined from what it initially was (started with Astra and switched to Claude just in the past week). The game is an RPG-themed tower defense mixed with tile matching, roguelite upgrades and dungeon editing or "growing".

I guess I need at least this level of complexity to find a game like this fun and keeping my attention.

So, thanks again for this actionable feedback which I do truly appreciate and will take into consideration. Cheers and happy gaming!

replies.author: AsparagusOk8818
replies.body:
https://preview.redd.it/ftw6v1nkkbwh1.png?width=1901&format=png&auto=webp&s=c2a25e0c9bd9eddd5eccbed1ddd57b7f9a5e6e4b

Here is the basic view when flying in X4. Do you see how most of the view is not dominated by buttons, and there is a clear language and intentionality to the interface? 

The way your eyes track the information flows naturally from the sparse central information, which is the most immediate and also the most engaging, to the denser information on the lower sides. And there are not one kajillion buttons on the screen. 

X4 understands that the player is going to be mapping their buttons and uses that as an opportunity for systems familiarization. It is shockingly clever.

  
And, my God in Heaven, no - 'this game isn't for everyone' is not a good excuse for bad UI design. Bad UI design is not a sign of complexity; it's just bad UI design. Bad UI design means the player doesn't even know if the game is for them or not because the interface is blocking them from even playing the game.

replies.author: LikeMyGame
replies.body:
In fairness, basic flying and shooting controls don't require much in the form of UI. You are comparing apples to oranges. And part of the learning curve with X4 is the massive amounts of key bindings needed to memorize/master in any given scenario. They just moved their "clutter" to the bindings behind the scenes.

My game requires those UI buttons and areas visible and actionable during gameplay because you can only use your mouse. You have to view the real-time map to see what the intruders are doing. You have to have the Ritual Forge (tile match making) always up to be planning your tile actions, you have to see your playable rites/actions...all of which require to be always present and visible as you can only interact with them via your mouse. You also want to have immediately visibility of your enemies stats.

I don't deny your opinion outright and will ponder your input. However, I disagree this is "just bad UI design". I believe part of the issue is that it is one part tower defense, one part tile matching and one part RPG-ish. There are a lot of elements to track and consider when playing the game.

Once again, this truly is not a game for everyone, but I do wholeheartedly agree that isn't an excuse for bad design. Point taken there.

comments.author: lark_devon
comments.body:
is there like a guide or something?   
Something I did for my game, was a quick tutorial, on what to do for folks that have never played my game

replies.author: LikeMyGame
replies.body:
Yes. I realized I needed a built-in tutorial mode. Initially, the gameplay depth was rather shallow and didn't need a tutorial. As the weeks went by and I envisioned new features and ways to make the gameplay more engrossing, I realized what was easy for me to understand (the creator) would not be so for others. The tutorial takes your hand and walks you through each major aspect of the game for people who are new.

That is why in the post I mentioned people should give the tutorial a try for the first time. On the surface, this seems like a simple game, but the truth is the mechanics can get deep. You don't have to get deep if you play on the easy levels, but the hardest level is impossible to beat without understanding the mechanics, forethought/planning and upgrading/building your dungeon to take on the Champions.
